title: Handoff and swarm
summary: In a handoff, one agent transfers control and the conversation to another agent that takes full ownership. Agents form a mesh with no central orchestrator, and each hop is a model call that can loop.
useIf: The right specialist is not known up front, emerges during the conversation, and should talk to the user directly.
avoidIf: The route is identifiable from the first message (use a router), you need one accountable owner, or work should run in parallel.

explain.md: **Handoff** means an agent decides to pass the task to another agent, and the receiver takes over. Microsoft Agent Framework describes handoff as a mesh topology with no central orchestrator: the receiving agent takes full ownership and has the full context, and handoff supports `Agent` only, with agents that support local tool execution [[r11]]. The Azure guide adds that agents in this pattern do not typically work in parallel, and full control moves from one agent to another [[r9]]. The OpenAI Agents SDK exposes a handoff to the model as a tool, named `transfer_to_<agent_name>` by default [[r20]].

explain.title: A handoff mesh with escape hatches
explain.alt: A user reaches a triage agent. Triage hands off to billing or technical agents. Specialists can return to triage or escalate to a human.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> T[Triage agent]
  T -->|transfer_to_billing| B[Billing agent]
  T -->|transfer_to_technical| X[Technical agent]
  B -->|back to triage| T
  X -->|back to triage| T
  B -->|escalate| H[Human agent]
  X -->|escalate| H

explain.md: Two design choices control behaviour. **State passing**: by default the next agent sees the history, but you can shape it. The Agents SDK offers `input_filter` to trim what the receiver sees, `input_type` for structured handoff arguments, `on_handoff` for side effects, `is_enabled` to switch a target on or off and `nest_handoff_history` [[r20]]. **Loop control**: The Azure guide lists infinite handoff loops and bouncing between agents as a risk [[r9]]. Handoff is interactive by default and returns to the user when an agent answers without handing off. Autonomous mode keeps an agent working until it hands off, a termination condition holds or the per-agent turn limit is hit, for example `WithAutonomousMode(turnLimit: 10)` in the C# builder [[r11]]. OpenAI's Swarm library introduced the idea of agents and handoffs and is labelled experimental and educational, replaced by the Agents SDK [[tr17]].

explain.title: Each handoff is a model call
explain.md: A conversation that hops through three specialists pays for three agent turns before the answer. Cap hops, define which agents may hand to which, and log every transfer with its reason.

whereToUse: Customer-support flows where a triage agent hands to billing, technical or account specialists
Domain tutors or advisors where the user converses with the specialist
Multi-skill assistants where expertise requirements appear during the conversation
Escalation paths that end in a human agent
Prototypes built on the Agents SDK or Agent Framework handoff orchestration

use: The best agent is unknown until the conversation reveals it
Specialists should own and continue the dialogue
A clear signal tells an agent it has reached its limit [[r9]]
avoid: The right agent is clear from the first input, so a deterministic router suffices [[r9]]
Poor routing would badly hurt the user experience
Avoiding loops and bouncing is hard to guarantee
flips: You need one accountable owner: use a supervisor with agents as tools
Multiple operations must run at once: use concurrent orchestration
Bouncing appears in traces: add a hop cap and an allow-list of handoff targets

pitfalls.symptom: A conversation bounces between two agents
pitfalls.cause: Each agent's instructions say the other is better suited, with no hop limit
pitfalls.fix: Set a hop cap, restrict handoff targets, add a termination condition and an escalate-to-human path.

pitfalls.symptom: The new agent repeats questions the user already answered
pitfalls.cause: History was filtered too hard or not passed at all
pitfalls.fix: Pass a structured summary of facts gathered, and use the history filter deliberately, not by default.

pitfalls.symptom: Hand-offs go to the wrong specialist
pitfalls.fix: Rewrite descriptions with clear boundaries, and evaluate handoff decisions on labelled conversations.

scenarios.title: Conversation that changes topic
scenarios.situation: A support assistant starts with account questions, and halfway through the user raises a billing dispute and then a technical fault. Specialists have different tools and policies. Users expect continuity.
constraints: User should talk to the specialist
Different tools and policies per specialist
unknowns: How many hops does a typical conversation need?
What state must pass between agents?
scenarios.question: What orchestration do you choose?

options.name: Handoff mesh with a hop cap, target allow-list, structured state passing and human escalation
options.why: Specialists take over the dialogue as topics change, and the guards contain the loop risk.
options.tradeoff: A model call per hop and a need to evaluate handoff decisions.

options.name: Supervisor with specialists as tools
options.why: One consistent voice and accountable owner.
options.tradeoff: Users never talk to the specialist, and every turn pays a hub hop.

options.name: A router that classifies only the first message
options.why: The topic changes later, so the first classification becomes wrong.
options.tradeoff: Right when the topic is fixed by the first message.

flips.if: Accountability must sit with one agent
flips.then: Use a supervisor and keep the specialist as a tool.
Tighten descriptions, cap hops and review routing evals.

scenarios.takeaway: Handoff fits conversations whose topic moves, if you cap the hops.

scenarios.title: Route known from the first message
scenarios.situation: An internal bot receives requests from a form that already tags the department. Latency matters, and each department has its own agent. No one expects the topic to change.
unknowns: Does the tag come from a trusted field?
What happens if a request is mistagged?
scenarios.question: How do you route?

options.name: Deterministic dispatcher on the form tag, with a fallback agent for mistagged requests
options.why: The route is known, so no model call is needed to choose, and latency stays low.
options.tradeoff: A mistagged request needs a fallback path.

options.name: Triage agent with handoff mesh
options.why: It adds a model hop and loop risk where a field lookup would do.
options.tradeoff: Right if the tag were missing or untrusted and content had to decide.

options.name: One agent with every department's tools
options.tradeoff: Tool overload and broad permissions in one agent.

flips.then: Add a classifier router before the department agents.

scenarios.takeaway: If code can pick the route, do not pay a model to pick it.

quiz.q: In the OpenAI Agents SDK, how is a handoff exposed to the model by default?
quiz.explain: Handoffs are modelled as tools, and the default tool name is transfer_to_ followed by the agent name, which you can override with tool_name_override. [[r20]]

quiz.q: Traces show conversations bouncing between two agents. Which changes address it?
options: Restrict which agents each agent may hand off to
Give both agents longer instructions about each other
quiz.explain: A cap, a target allow-list and a termination condition are the named controls for loops. Longer mutual instructions often make bouncing worse. [[r11]]

flashcards.front: What does the receiving agent get in an Agent Framework handoff?
flashcards.back: Full ownership of the task and the full context. It is a mesh topology with no central orchestrator [[r11]].

flashcards.front: Name four handoff options in the OpenAI Agents SDK.
flashcards.back: tool_name_override, on_handoff, input_type and input_filter, plus is_enabled, tool_description_override and nest_handoff_history [[r20]].
Experimental and educational, replaced by the OpenAI Agents SDK, per its README checked 2026-10-13 [[tr17]].
